say: You give it a model that uses $e^x$, $\ln x$ or trig, such as a temperature or a population. It finds the **rate of change** at a moment, or where the model is largest or smallest.
The key idea: the derivative is the rate. Differentiate the model first, then put the number in.

how.higher: It turned up once in 2020, as a Paper 1 part: differentiate an exponential model and use the derivative to find when the growth passes a value.

example.question: The temperature of a drink is $T = 70e^{-0.05t}$ degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after it is poured. Find the rate at which the temperature is changing after $10$ minutes.

steps.title: Differentiate the model
steps.say: A rate is a derivative. Differentiate $T$ with respect to $t$. The $e^{-0.05t}$ stays, and the $-0.05$ multiplies in front.

steps.title: Put in the time
steps.say: You want the rate when $t = 10$. Put $10$ into $\hl{1}{T'(t)}$.

steps.title: Say what it means
steps.say: The answer is negative, so the temperature is falling. Give the unit.

lines.text: The drink is cooling at $2.12$ degrees Celsius per minute.

higher.tip: Show the derivative before you substitute. The marks start when $N'(t)$ is stated.
If you leave out the differentiation, you get no credit, even with a correct number from the model.
Write the derivative with the number fully put in, even if you stop there. That earns high partial credit.
When you solve an exponential equation, take logs and write the equation in your unknown. That step is marked.

say: You give it a polynomial, such as $2x^3 - 5x^2 + 4$. It gives back $f'(x)$, the formula for the **slope** at any point.
The key idea: take each term on its own. Bring the power down to multiply, then take one off the power. A number on its own becomes $0$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it all the time as a step inside bigger questions on Paper 1: finding a rate, a tangent slope or a turning point, and sometimes as a part of its own worth 5 marks.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 1 in most years, as a short part worth 5 or 10 marks that leads on to a slope, a tangent or a turning point.

example.question: Differentiate $f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 8$ and find the slope of the graph at $x = 2$.

steps.title: Differentiate each term
steps.say: Take one term at a time. Multiply by the power, then lower the power by one. Write down the derivative of the number term too.

lines.text: The $-8$ differentiates to $0$. Write that in: the marks need it shown.

steps.title: Put in x = 2
steps.say: The slope at $x = 2$ is $\hl{1}{f'(2)}$. Put $2$ into the derivative.

higher.tip: Differentiation must be used. If you do not differentiate, you get no credit.

sources.quote: No credit if differentiation is not

higher.tip: You do not have to simplify the derivative. An unsimplified correct answer still gets full marks.

sources.quote: Accept the answer in an unsimplified

higher.tip: Even if you slip, differentiate the terms you can. One correct term earns partial credit.
Get every term right. Two correct terms earns high partial credit.

ordinary.tip: Write down the derivative of the number term. If it is not shown, those marks are not awarded.

sources.quote: differentiation of independent term must be explicit

ordinary.tip: Get as many terms right as you can. Two terms correctly differentiated earns high partial credit.
Differentiate the terms you can. Any correct differentiation earns partial credit.
If you go on to a tangent, finish by rearranging the line. Leaving it unrearranged loses a mark.

sources.quote: fails to rearrange equation of the line

say: You give it $f(x)$. It differentiates **twice** and gives $f''(x)$, the rate at which the slope is changing.
The key idea: just differentiate the derivative. The sign of $f''$ tells you whether a turning point is a maximum or a minimum.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step in Paper 1 questions: to classify a turning point, or to find where a rate is changing fastest.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it rarely, in a Paper 1 part where the second derivative is set to $0$ to find a point.

example.question: Find $f''(x)$ for $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 5x$, and find the value of $x$ for which $f''(x) = 0$.

steps.title: Differentiate once
steps.say: Differentiate $f(x)$ to get the first derivative.

steps.title: Differentiate again
steps.say: Now differentiate the first derivative. That gives $\hl{1}{f''(x)}$.

steps.title: Set it to zero
steps.say: You want $f''(x) = 0$. Set $\hl{1}{f''(x)}$ equal to $0$ and solve for $x$.

higher.tip: Say you are using the second derivative. Writing it down earns low partial credit.
Find the second derivative first. Finding it correctly earns high partial credit.
To find where a quantity changes fastest, set the second derivative to zero. State that step.
When a quadratic gives two answers, say which one you keep. Writing both unexplained loses a mark.

ordinary.tip: Differentiate with care. Any correct differentiation earns partial credit.
Always use differentiation to find a turning point. Without it you get no marks.

sources.quote: If differentiation is not used, award zero marks

say: You give it a root or a reciprocal, like $\sqrt{x}$ or $\frac{1}{x^2}$. It gives back the derivative, using the same power rule as for $x^n$.
The key idea: first **rewrite** the root or fraction as a power of $x$. Then bring the power down and take one off it.

how.higher: It shows up inside Paper 1 questions on differentiation, as a part worth 5 marks, or as a step towards a turning point.

steps.title: Write as powers
steps.say: A root is a power of $\frac{1}{2}$. A reciprocal is a negative power. Rewrite both so the rule applies.

steps.title: Use the power rule
steps.say: Bring each power down to multiply. Then take one off each power to get $\hl{1}{f'(x)}$.

steps.title: Write it back
steps.say: Turn the negative and fractional powers back into a root and a fraction.

higher.tip: Any correct differentiation earns partial credit, so rewrite as powers and differentiate what you can.
If you use the quotient rule, substitute carefully. A correct substitution earns high partial credit.
A negative power in the answer is accepted. You need not turn it back into a fraction.
